# Prompt Compilation

## Purpose
Assemble the prompt package for a shot deterministically from its sources —
character/location/prop bibles, the shot file, the style bible, and the
reference plan — translated into the target provider's dialect, so the same
inputs always compile to the same prompt.

## Use When
- A shot has an approved reference plan and generation is next.
- Switching a shot to a different provider (recompile, don't rewrite).
- A generated result reveals the prompt contradicted a bible — fix the source, recompile.

## Inputs
- `production/scenes/<SC_ID>/shots/SH_*.yaml` and `references/reference-plan.yaml`.
- Bibles: character.yaml, wardrobe.yaml, location.yaml, prop.yaml, style bible.
- Provider capabilities and dialect from `manifests/*-providers.json`.

## Process
1. Verify sources: shot approved, reference plan present, cited masters valid.
   Refuse to compile from memory or improvisation — every phrase must trace to
   a source file.
2. Split labor between text and images: identity, wardrobe detail, set
   geometry, and prop appearance are carried by reference images from the plan;
   text carries action, camera, composition, lighting state, and style — plus
   exact descriptions for any reference the plan marked as overflow.
3. Draw phrasing verbatim from bibles (canonical descriptor strings, style
   keyword block); never introduce new adjectives at compile time.
4. Order the text by provider weighting: subject and action first, then camera
   (size, angle, height, lens, movement), then environment/state, then style.
5. Apply the provider dialect: veo favors fluent cinematographic sentences and
   explicit camera verbs; kling favors compact clause lists and strong motion
   phrases; runway expects terse imperative style with camera keywords;
   seedance takes structured descriptive sentences with timing cues; generic
   emits neutral comma-separated blocks any backend can consume.
6. Compile negatives/exclusions: the style bible's forbidden terms plus the
   plan's contradiction guards (e.g. wrong wardrobe), mapped to the provider's
   negative mechanism — or folded into positive phrasing when unsupported.
7. Attach reference entries (asset paths, weights, crops) from the plan only;
   enforce the provider's reference cap and aspect/duration limits.
8. Write the package with source hashes (shot, plan, bible versions) and
   validate against `schemas/prompt-package.schema.json` before saving.

## Outputs
- `production/scenes/<SC_ID>/prompts/<provider>/SH_*.yaml` and mirrored entries
  under `production/prompts/` (`prompt-package.schema.json`).

## Quality Bar
- Every text token traces to a bible, shot file, or plan entry.
- No image-carried fact is restated in text in a way that could contradict it.
- Package validates against the schema and the provider's capabilities.
- Recompiling with unchanged sources is byte-identical.

## Common Failure Modes
- Freehanding "improvements" into the prompt instead of fixing the bible.
- Re-describing a referenced face in text, fighting the identity image.
- One prompt reused across providers, ignoring dialect and caps.
- Negatives listing things the shot actually needs (over-broad exclusion).

## Notes
`scripts/compile-prompts.js` automates this procedure; manual compilation must
follow the same rules. If a prompt keeps failing, the defect is upstream — in
the bible, plan, or shot — and that is where the edit goes.

Lens tokens are provider-gated per the vendors' own guides
(`scripts/lib/lens-language.js`, `docs/research/lens-language.md`): Veo wants
cinematography language — including lens and focus — at the head of the
prompt; FLUX-class image models are lens-literal (numeric focal lengths and
f-stops measurably shape output); Runway Gen-4 video prompts are motion-only,
so its lens look is carried entirely by the conditioning keyframe. The
compiler applies these policies; never hand-add lens text against them.
